title: When Your Worth Is Your Work: Why Success Never Feels Like Enough
summary: Learn how tying self-worth to work and achievement can lead to perfectionism, burnout, stress and anxiety, and discover practical ways to build healthier self-worth.
body_markdown:
One of the things I notice most in my work is how rarely success feels like enough to the people achieving it. Not because they’re ungrateful or difficult, but because their sense of being okay as a person has become quietly dependent on their performance. This article explores what that pattern looks like, what it costs, and what actually helps.


I work with a lot of high achievers. People who are genuinely good at what they do, who have built careers most would envy, and who still find it almost impossible to feel like enough. Not sometimes. Consistently.


A client I worked with recently described it better than I could. He’d had an exceptional year, a major promotion, a successful project, glowing feedback from his board. And yet he came to my first session describing himself as “fine, just tired,”[feeling flat and irritable](https://mindfi.co/blog/when-everything-looks-fine-but-something-still-feels-off) , increasingly distant from his partner, who had told him gently that it felt like he was never really home, even when he was home. He didn’t see a problem with his work ethic. It had gotten him everything he had. What he wanted help with was the flatness.


What he was describing has a name. Psychologists call it the arrival fallacy, the belief that reaching a goal will produce lasting fulfilment, followed by the discovery that it doesn’t. Tal Ben-Shahar described it from his own experience as a competitive athlete. Winning brought a brief lift, and then “the same stress and pressure and emptiness returned” (Ben-Shahar, 2007). Research confirms this is structural, not personal. People tend to return to their usual mood much faster than they expect to after positive events (Diener, Lucas, & Scollon, 2006). The achievement itself isn’t the problem. The problem is what so many high achievers are quietly expecting it to do, which is to finally make them feel like enough.


That gap is what research into contingent worth is about. For many high achievers, their sense of being a worthy, capable person isn’t a stable internal resource. It’s something that has to be earned again, over and over, through performance, which is exactly why the feeling never lasts. This isn’t narcissism, and it isn’t a character flaw. It’s a learned pattern. And in my experience, it’s one of the most common and most costly things I see.


## **What Is Contingent Worth?**


Research has long focused on whether someone has high or low self regard. But there’s another dimension that matters just as much, which is what that sense of self is built on (Crocker & Wolfe, 2001). For many high achievers, it’s built on competence and competition, on being good at what they do and being better than the people around them.


There’s an important distinction here. Feeling good because you did something well is a healthy response to achievement. But feeling like a good or acceptable person only when you do something well means your sense of who you are has become conditional. And conditional things are, by definition, unstable. Research on motivation also shows that when people work primarily to escape guilt or shame rather than because the work genuinely matters to them, it creates a very different kind of pressure, one that doesn’t ease with success (Ryan & Deci, 2000).


## **The Cost**


It’s tempting to write this off as the price of ambition, uncomfortable but worth it. In my experience, it rarely is. And the research backs that up.


### ***On your mental health***


When performance wobbles, a missed target, a bad quarter, an illness that takes you out of action, people whose sense of worth depends on performance don’t just experience a setback. Research on students shows that those who tie how they feel about themselves to performance see their depressive symptoms spike significantly more than their peers during periods of high stress, even when their baseline wellbeing looks identical (Schöne et al., 2015). There is good reason to think the same dynamic plays out in adult high achievers. This is why so many of the people I work with describe these moments not as setbacks, but as something closer to an identity crisis.


Perfectionism plays into this too. Holding yourself to high standards isn’t the problem. But believing that other people expect you to be perfect, and that their regard depends on it, is consistently linked to burnout, anxiety, and depression (Hewitt & Flett, 1991). It’s exhausting in a way that simply wanting to do good work never is.


### ***On your body***


Chronic psychological stress doesn’t stay psychological. Research consistently links high perceived stress to increased cardiovascular risk over time (Richardson et al., 2012). When the body’s stress response stays switched on indefinitely, it takes a toll on blood sugar, inflammation, and the blood vessels themselves. Constantly feeling like your worth is on the line isn’t just hard on the mind. It’s hard on the heart.


### ***On your relationships***


Research on workaholism, meaning compulsive overworking driven by inner need rather than enjoyment, finds that it predicts burnout even when the actual job demands are controlled for (Clark et al., 2016). Studies also show workaholics often don’t report their relationships as damaged. Their partners tell a different story, reporting significantly more estrangement and less warmth than partners of people who are not workaholics (Robinson et al., 2001; Bakker et al., 2009). The cost is real, but it’s often invisible to the person paying it, and that invisibility is part of what makes it so hard to address.


## **It’s Not Just You. It’s Also the Environment.**


Something I find myself saying often in sessions is that no amount of insight fully protects you if the environment around you is actively rewarding the pattern you’re trying to change. Research has identified what’s called an overwork climate, which is an unspoken organisational belief that long hours are normal and expected. It has the strongest effect on people who already have traits driven by achievement (Mazzetti et al., 2014). An overwork climate doesn’t just tolerate these tendencies. It amplifies them.


The same is true of your social world. If the people around you share the unspoken rule that busyness equals worth, that worldview gets quietly reinforced every time you’re together. Sometimes the most important decision isn’t a mindset shift. It’s honestly assessing whether your environment is compatible with the kind of life you’re trying to build — including[the hidden question beneath workplace stress](https://mindfi.co/blog/the-hidden-question-beneath-workplace-stress) .


## **The Recovery Paradox**


Research shows that mentally switching off from work during time away from work is a core recovery mechanism, not a luxury but how the system is supposed to function (Sonnentag & Fritz, 2015). Here’s the catch. The people under the most stress are often the least able to do it, because high stress makes thoughts about work more intrusive and harder to quiet (Sonnentag, 2018). Researchers call this the recovery paradox. I’d put it more simply. The people who most need a break are the ones least able to take one — the same pattern as[when stress becomes the baseline](https://mindfi.co/blog/when-stress-becomes-the-baseline) .


“Just relax” rarely works because the capacity to switch off has already been eroded by the very thing it’s meant to fix. In my work, the first step is often the most basic one. Creating protected time and space away from the usual environment. Not to plan or optimise, but to have enough distance to notice what’s actually going on.


## **Treating Yourself With Compassion: The Ingredient Most High Achievers Avoid**


Almost every client I’ve worked with who achieves at a high level carries some version of the same belief. If I stop being hard on myself, I’ll stop being driven. Being critical of yourself becomes the engine. Soften it, and the whole thing stalls.


Research consistently says the opposite. Treating yourself with the same understanding you’d offer a friend who was struggling is associated with lower depression, anxiety, and fear of failure, and with higher resilience and motivation (Neff, 2023). People who are high in compassion toward themselves still pursue ambitious goals. They just do it from a place of genuine interest rather than fear of falling short (Neff et al., 2005).


Treating yourself with compassion isn’t about lowering standards. It’s about no longer treating every setback as evidence of your fundamental worth as a person. That shift from performance as proof to performance as expression changes everything about how the drive feels, and what it costs you.


## **A Few Questions Worth Sitting With**


I often ask clients versions of these questions early in my sessions. Not to answer perfectly, just to notice the honest first reaction.


When you finish something significant, how long does the satisfaction last before the next target appears?


On a scale of 0 to 10, how much does your sense of being a good person depend on how the last week at work went?


If nothing about your performance changed for a whole week, no wins, no losses, how would you feel about yourself by the end of it?


Whose disapproval are you most afraid of if you were to genuinely scale back?


If several of these produced an uncomfortable “huh,” that’s useful information. It’s also exactly the kind of thing that’s easier to explore with someone else than to untangle alone.


## **Back to the Executive**


The client from the opening came into his first session expecting to talk about time management. Instead, I asked him one simple question. On a scale of 0 to 10, how much does your sense of being a good, capable person depend on how the last week at work went? He paused for a long time, then said he’d honestly put it at an eight or nine.


We looked for exceptions, moments where that number had felt lower. He described a weekend away with no laptop, where for about a day he’d felt normal before the pull to check in crept back. That one day became a clue. It wasn’t that he was incapable of feeling okay without performing. He’d almost never given himself the chance to find out.


I asked the miracle question. If your sense of being okay wasn’t riding on the next deliverable, what would your partner notice first? His answer was immediate. That I wasn’t checking my phone during dinner. That I was actually listening.


His first steps were small. One protected evening a week with no devices, decided in advance. A daily practice of noticing when his mood was tracking his last win or loss at work. And an honest look at his team’s culture, where he realised he’d been one of the people modelling the very behaviour he wanted to change. None of this touched his ambition. What shifted was the foundation underneath it.


## **Where to Go From Here**


If any of this feels uncomfortably familiar, that’s not a verdict. It’s information. In my work, four directions tend to help most.


Look honestly at your environment. Ask whether your workplace or social circle is rewarding the exact pattern you’re trying to shift, because no amount of inner work fully overcomes a current that strong.


Create protected recovery time before anything else. Given the recovery paradox, this has to come first and it has to be protected deliberately, not saved for whenever you find the time, because for most people that time never comes.


Notice the pattern, gently. A daily practice of observing, without judgment, when your mood is tracking your last win or loss makes the pattern visible. You can’t loosen a grip you can’t see.


Build compassion toward yourself as a skill, not just a mood. This isn’t about positive thinking. It’s about responding to your own setbacks the way you’d respond to someone you respected having a hard week.


The drive that got you here doesn’t need to go. What’s worth examining is what it’s resting on, and whether that foundation can hold the weight indefinitely.
